title: The bee (49–52)
hook: as the bee takes nectar and leaves the flower unharmed; look to your own faults, not others'
tomorrow: The lotus on the rubbish heap (53–59)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the garland-maker, who chooses well from the basket. Your line was pick the flower.

Watch a bee in a garden for one minute. It lands on a flower, pushes in, takes what it came for, and lifts off. Then look at the flower. Same petals, same color, same scent, still open for the next bee. If anything, it's better off: the bee carried its pollen along. A lot of taking doesn't work that way: something is used up, bruised, left worse. The Dhammapada watched the same garden and found a whole way of living in it.
screen: `ONE MINUTE WITH A BEE.` → `THE FLOWER IS STILL THERE.` → `A WHOLE WAY OF LIVING.`

segments.voice: Verse forty-nine, in Müller's English: “As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village.” The first picture is a monk on his alms round. He walks into the village, receives a little food from each house, and leaves without being a burden to anyone: taking only what's offered, leaving every household as whole as he found it. But the verse reaches anyone who depends on others, which is everyone. Can you take what you need, from your family, your coworkers, the earth, and leave them unharmed? Verse fifty turns the bee's attention inward. Don't look at the faults of others, it says, what they've done and left undone. Look at what you yourself have done and left undone. The bee doesn't inspect the flower for flaws. It takes the nectar and goes. Then verses fifty-one and fifty-two, a twin pair about words. Verse fifty-one: “Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly.” Verse fifty-two is the flower with color and scent: good words from someone who lives them. You met that idea in the cowherd; the flower chapter gives it a new picture. So the bee teaches three things. Take without harming. Mind your own faults, not the flower's. And let your words carry some scent: something lived behind them.
screen: `TAKE, AND LEAVE THE FLOWER WHOLE.` · `THE MONK ON HIS ALMS ROUND.` · `YOUR OWN FAULTS, NOT OTHERS'.` · `A FLOWER WITHOUT SCENT.` · then, large: `THE BEE LEAVES THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Think of the places you'll take something from today: food from the kitchen, time and help from a coworker, patience from someone at home, water, power, a seat on the bus. For each, imagine being the bee, taking what you need and leaving it whole: a thank-you, cleaning up after yourself, not taking the last of something. Choose one place, and hold that picture while you breathe.
The bee. Taking the nectar and leaving the flower unharmed: living among others without using them up.
Your line: the bee leaves the flower. Nectar taken, the flower left whole. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada monks still go on alms rounds, receiving small amounts of food from many households, and teachers cite the bee verse as a picture of taking from the world without harm.

fork.setup: you're a monk on alms round. one house is poor and offers only a spoonful of rice. what fits the bee?
options: receive it gladly and move on, taking only what's offered.
fork.reveal: the bee takes a little and leaves the flower whole. the alms round spreads the need so no house is burdened.

original.note: Pali: bee, from verse forty-nine: 'yathapi bhamaro puppham.'

trapdoor: what you thought: the bee verse is a nice nature picture.

what a scholar hears: 'muni' in verse 49 is the sage or silent one, and 'game care' means wandering in the village for alms; the commentary tells it with the miserly treasurer Kosiya.
